Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 1 of 29 Fir No. : 397/2008 Police Station : R.K. Puram Under section. : 498/A304B/34, Ipc Date of Assignment : 30.09.2010 Reserved for Judgment on : 24.01.2015 Date of Judgment : 27.02.2015 State vs . Amod Kumar Mishra And Ors. 1 Of 29 on 27 February, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/14829880/ 1 Judgment 1. An information that a lady has committed suicide was received in the police station R K Puram through DD No.14A on 12.10.2008, which brought the police machinery into action. SI Rajesh Kumar, who was deputed to the spot found that deceased Nutan was married barely a year ago and, therefore, he ensured that the parents of the deceased were informed. He got the site inspected through the crime team, which was called at the spot. The body was removed to the hospital and needful was got done. 2. On 14.10.2008 father of the deceased namely Upender Kumar Jha came to Delhi and gave his statement to the Executive Magistrate whereby he informed that deceased Nutan was married to Amod Kumar Mishra on 22.02.2008 with the consent of both the families. The usual ceremonies were performed in respect to the marriage, however, he alleged that Nutan was being tortured and State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 2 of 29 harassed for various reasons, primarily belonging to rural background and for not bringing enough dowry. The harassment gradually exceeded from verbal assault to physical assault. He had even transmitted a sum of Rs.75,000/ in three installments of Rs. 30,000/, 20,000/ and 25,000/ to meet the demand and in order to make the life of his daughter Nutan comfortable. The harassment and torture, however, continued and the deceased Nutan confided about this to her sister, who too was living in Delhi and other family members. Father of the deceased conveyed to the authorities that his daughter Nutan was killed by her husband, his brother i.e. Amod Kumar and Pramod Kumar respectively, Sunita, sisterinlaw and Taruna Devi, motherinlaw of the deceased, as it was the harassment and torture perpetuated by them which drove Nutan to commit suicide. Based upon such statement an FIR was registered. Kashinath Jha (Mausa of Amod Mishra and Pramod Mishra) was also blamed and thereafter he too was arraigned in the list of accused persons. The investigation ultimately culminated into the chargesheet filed under section 304B/498A/34 IPC. 3. After compliance of section 207 Cr.P.C., the case was committed to the Court of Sessions. Based upon the allegations and the investigation carried out, prima facie case under section State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 3 of 29 304B/498/34 IPC was found against the aforesaid five accused persons i.e. Amod Mishra, Pramod Mishra, Arti, Taruna and Kashinath Jha and accordingly a charge was framed qua all of them, to which they pleaded not guilty. 4. With a view to substantiate the allegations, the prosecution arrayed 28 witnesses in the list of witnesses and practically managed to examine all totaling to 25 of them and thereafter evidence was concluded by the prosecution. 5. The evidence coming on record was put to the accused persons in order to have their version of the incident and their explanation and reaction of the evidence. As expected, while controverting the evidence against them in the shape of statements under section 313 Cr.P.C., all the accused persons claimed themselves to be innocent and opted to bring evidence in their defence and examined 19 witnesses and thereafter concluded their evidence. texts.arguments: 7. It is asserted by learned Additional Public Prosecutor that there is evidence to the effect that the deceased was being harassed for the purpose of dowry and harassment ,which went to the extent of physical torture, bring the acts of the accused persons into the realm of section 498A IPC. It is further submitted that the death since had occurred within the seven years of marriage, therefore, not only the presumption comes into play but gets fortified in view of the evidence coming on record that the deceased was being harassed and tortured for the purpose of dowry. In any case, it is submitted that the accused persons are unable to ward off or upset the presumption and therefore the prosecution is able to drive home its case. 8. Counsel for the accused persons, on the other hand, have come up with the contentions that the evidence has been brought on record to the effect that the matrimonial life of the deceased was trouble free, cordial and she was living in a very comfortable atmosphere with the other family members. There was no question of demand of dowry and in fact nothing was demanded nor was required by the accused persons. It is further submitted by counsels State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 5 of 29 for the accused persons that the allegations are vague, generic in nature not specifying the incident, date and time and so general that each and every person living there in Delhi has been roped in. The deceased was pregnant and evidence is brought to the effect that she was not only being looked after very well but was being regularly taken up for medical checkups. 9. It is also attempted to be brought by the prosecution that the victim was not only harassed physically and mentally but was compelled to household chores. In this context, it is submitted that the maid was engaged by the family, who was regularly coming for regular household works, therefore, there is no question of compelling the deceased. With these contentions, it is submitted that the atmosphere at the house of accused was cordial and pleasant. Parents of the deceased had also visited the deceased almost immediately after the marriage and after coming to Delhi and stayed with the family for sometime. The mother of the deceased stayed in Delhi for about three months for her treatment and assistance was extended by accused persons in this context too. The family had even gone for outings local as well as outside Delhi. In these circumstances, the cordiality and pleasant atmosphere in the family can be very well inferred. Thus, when the accused State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 6 of 29 persons are otherwise well endowed with the material things then there was no need for them to ask for the pittance in the shape of Rs.80,000/ or One Lakh that too for the purpose of purchasing a car. It is asserted that the family had a car already and an official vehicle was also provided to Pramod. Demand of Rs. One Lakh or Two Lakhs, which allegedly was there, could not have fetched any car, therefore, all these go to show that the accused persons have been falsely implicated out of vengeance and vendetta. 10. Another example of false implication has been put forth by counsel for the accused persons when it is submitted that the incident took place on 12.10.2008 and the statement of the father of the deceased was recorded on 14.10.2008 giving enough time not only to introspect but to consult also. At this stage, it was pointed out that the brotherinlaw (Jija) of the deceased is a lawyer based in State vs . Amod Kumar Mishra And Ors. 1 Of 29 on 27 February, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/14829880/ 3 Delhi. To emphasize this aspect, it is asserted State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 7 of 29 that the bill of the jewellery brought in by the father of the deceased contains a mobile phone number, which number has turned out to be incorrect in the light of the evidence of the officials of the BSNL namely Mohd. Asif Hussain, examined as DW17, who deposed on the strength of customer application form and other documents that the mobile phone number 9470213476 was allotted to Sh. Om Prakash Gupta on 11.07.2008 and was activated on the same day. 11. In order to drive home its case under sections 498A and 304 IPC, the prosecution has to prove that the victim was treated with cruelty as defined under section 498A and that such a treatment was with a view to seek dowry and as regards section 304B IPC is concerned the prosecution has to establish the following facts: i) the death of a woman must have been caused by burns or bodily injury or otherwise than under normal circumstances; ii) such death must have occurred within seven years of her marriage; State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 8 of 29 iii) the woman must have been subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or by relatives of her husband; iv) such cruelty or harassment must be for or in connection with demand for dowry; v) such cruelty or harassment is shown to have been meted out to the woman soon before her death. 12. It could thus be seen that the death should be unnatural within seven years of marriage where the woman was subjected to cruel treatment soon before her death for the purpose of demand of dowry. Reference in this context can be made to the judgment in Kaliyaperumal v. State of Tamil Nadu, AIR 2003 SC 3828." For the purpose of cruelty/ harassment, the explanation attached to section 498A may be looked into, which goes as under : Explanation. For the purpose of this section, ''cruelty'' means State vs . Amod Kumar Mishra And Ors. 1 Of 29 on 27 February, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/14829880/ 4 (a) any willful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand. Expression 'soon before her death': meaning of "The expression 'soon before her death' used in the substantive section 304B, IPC and section 113B of the Evidence Act is State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 9 of 29 present with the idea of proximity text. No definite period has been indicated and the expression 'soon before her death' is not defined. There must be existence of a proximate and livelink between the effect of cruelty based on dowry demand and the concerned death. 17. The judgment in State of West Bengal v. Orilal Jaiswal and anr., : (1994) 1 SCC 73 can be looked into where the following observations were made by the Hon'ble Apex Court: We are not oblivious that in a criminal trial the degree of proof is stricter than what is required in a civil proceedings. The requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt does not stand altered even after the introduction of section 498A IPC and section 113A of the Indian State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 13 of 29 Evidence Act. Lord Denning in Bater Vs. Bater, 1950 (2) AII ER 458, 459 has observed that the doubt must of a reasonable man and the standard adopted be a standard adopted by a reasonable and just man for coming to a conclusion considering the particular subject matter. 27. In this context, reference can be made to the judgment in State of U.P. Vs. Ramesh Kumar Barnwal & Ors. 2008 (1) ACR 818 where it has been observed as follows : It is very common and probable and Court can take notice of the fact that when there is a mediator through whom marriage has been performed and subsequently shortly after the marriage there is any trouble arising out of the said marriage as in the present case, in the absence of any special reason, parties do approach the mediator for help and the aggrieved party definitely complains him about the conduct of the other side. In Kans Raj v. State of Punjab and Ors. MANU/SC/0296/2000 : AIR 2000 SC 2324 the Hon'ble Supreme Court, inter alia, observed as under; In cases where such accusations are State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 27 of 29 made, the overt acts attributed to persons other than husband are required to be proved beyond reasonable doubt. A tendency has, however, developed for roping in all relations of the in State vs . Amod Kumar Mishra And Ors. 1 Of 29 on 27 February, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/14829880/ 11 laws of the deceased wives in the matters of dowry deaths which, if not discouraged, is likely to affect the case of the prosecution even against the real culprits. State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 28 of 29 37.
